messages:
maria: FYI incoming escalation from Acme; they started using 64k context and report a mix of 429 rate_limit_exceeded and occasional 401 auth failures when they switch model variants. Symptoms: sustained 429 spikes during batch runs (~800 RPM), per-request latency occasionally >2.5s, and some requests showing 0 tokens consumed in billing UI. Can we triage?

ryan: Can you paste a minimal repro (curl) and one full response (headers + body) showing the 429 and the 401? Need request-id/timestamps so we can look in logs. Also: which exact model string are they calling?

maria: Here's the snippet they sent paraphrased (sanitized):
```bash
curl -X POST https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate 
  -H "Authorization: Bearer sk-ACME..." 
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" 
  -d '{"model":"rwd-4x","input":"<~60k token prompt>","max_tokens":512}'
```
Their returned response (trimmed):
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
x-request-id: rq_0a1b2c3d
content-type: application/json
content-length: 138
x-ratelimit-rpm-limit: 1200
x-ratelimit-rpm-remaining: 0
x-ratelimit-concurrency-limit: 24
x-ratelimit-concurrency-remaining: 0
{ "error": "rate_limit_exceeded", "message":"per-model throttle: rpm exhausted" }

They also saw a 401 once after rotating token: HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized, body: {"error":"invalid_api_key"} but token worked for other endpoints. Billing UI shows a couple requests with 0 token usage which is confusing to them.

divya: Thanks. A few quick notes: 1) Long contexts count more heavily against internal scheduling / concurrency (we down-prioritize very long contexts to keep latency SLOs). 2) Per-model RPM/TPM and concurrency are enforced cumulatively; a 64k context consumes GPU memory and reduces effective concurrent slots, so the same RPM can exhaust capacity faster. 3) 0 token entries in UI often mean the request was short-circuited server-side (throttled) before billing meters; we'll confirm.

ryan: Repro checklist for eng-ml/infra:
- request-id (from x-request-id) and exact server timestamps (give timezone)
- full raw response headers + body for a 429 and a successful request before/after the spike
- the customer's concurrency pattern (do they fan out many simultaneous requests?)
- whether they used the same API key across processes or rotated keys
- example prompt length in tokens (tokenized) and sample input so we can run against test infra

maria: Provided rq_0a1b2c3d and three adjacent timestamps (2025-11-02T14:12:11Z, 14:12:14Z, 14:12:20Z). They say they had ~60 concurrent jobs all using the same key.

divya: That explains it — same-key fanout + long context is a worst-case for per-model limits. Two mitigation paths: client side (add jitter/backoff + token-based queueing) or server-side (we can enable fallback routing to rwd-4x-quant or reduce effective per-request concurrency via our QoS policy). For immediate relief: ask them to reduce concurrency to <20 or spread across API keys while we investigate.

maria: Customer tried exponential backoff but still got bursts of 429s during heavy runs. They want automatic fallback to a compatible model when throttle happens. Is that safe?

ryan: We do support automatic fallback in routing layer but only to variants with similar output distribution. Eng-ML can whitelist the rwd-4x-quant fallback for them temporarily. I'll open an infra ticket if you confirm repro steps. Also recommend they check the Console -> Usage -> Per-model quotas page; it shows a per-model RPM and concurrency cap (and burst window size).

infra-bot: [alert] per-model-throttle: model=rwd-4x spike_window=10m peak_rpm=1350 threshold=1000 triggered at 2025-11-02T14:12:20Z (link: /alerts/ALRT-9821)

divya: For the 401: that usually means the token was invalidated mid-run (maybe rotation). Ask them to verify the token used on the failing requests matches the one in Console -> API Keys and that they haven't hit account-level auth throttles. If they rotated keys in the middle of a fanout, some processes could still be using the old key and get 401s intermittently.

maria: Action plan I'm proposing to Acme: 1) Reduce concurrency to 15 and add jittered exponential backoff (we can share a code sample). 2) Send full tokenized prompt + request-ids so eng-ml can repro on canary. 3) Optionally enable fallback to rwd-4x-quant for this customer for the next 72h. 4) Check API key rotation timing. They asked for a quick code snippet for backoff — draft below.

ryan: Sample backoff pseudocode to share (short):
```python
# simple jittered backoff
for attempt in range(max_retries):
  resp = send_request()
  if resp.status_code == 429:
    sleep = base * (2 ** attempt) * random.uniform(0.8, 1.2)
    time.sleep(min(sleep, max_backoff))
  else:
    break
```
Also call out: treat 401/403 as immediate stop for that worker until key is confirmed.

divya: I'll take the eng-ml side once we get the tokenized prompt. I'll also check telemetry for any meter gaps that could explain the "0 tokens" rows in UI. If we confirm a metering bug we'll escalate to billing.

maria: Sent to customer: please paste the tokenized prompt length (token count), the sample prompt (or a sanitized version), and the x-request-id values. I'll enable a short-term fallback after we get confirmation.

ryan: TL;DR: root cause likely fanout with same key + long context -> effective concurrency exhaustion -> per-model RPM/concurrency throttle. Short-term: reduce concurrency, enable fallback variant, add jittered backoff. Long-term: consider dedicated capacity or reserved quota if they need sustained high throughput with large contexts.

maria: thanks — I'll follow up once Acme replies. :thumbsup:

divya: assigning to eng-ml (divya) — will update within 4 hours. :white_check_mark:
